title: How to Edit These Notes
text: 你平时只需要编辑扩展名为 .qmd 的源文件。它和 Markdown 几乎一样，但对数学公式、目录和提示框支持得更好。侧边栏、首页卡片、主题目录和 HTML 都由 Quarto 根据这些源文件自动生成。

title: How to Edit These Notes
text:
修改一篇笔记
在 VS Code 左侧文件列表中打开对应的 .qmd 文件，直接修改文字并保存即可：
## A new section

普通文字写在这里，行内公式写成 $X \to Y$。

$$
\Omega_{X/Y}=0
$$
以 --- 包围的文件开头是页面信息。每篇正式笔记都需要填写：
---
title: "A New Note"
subtitle: ""
description: "A short description shown on the topic page."
order: 80
---

title 是页面标题以及侧边栏中的名称。
description 是主题目录中显示的一句话简介。
order 是阅读顺序，必须写成数字。现有页面以 10 为间隔排列，因此可以把新页面插入中间，例如在 40 和 50 之间使用 45。
subtitle 可以留空。

修改并保存后，本地预览会自动重新生成相应的 HTML。

title: How to Edit These Notes
text:
删除一篇笔记
删除对应的 .qmd 文件即可。下一次预览或构建时，Quarto 会自动把它从侧边栏和主题目录移除。
如果其他笔记的正文中手动链接了被删除的页面，那些正文链接仍需自行修改。

title: How to Edit These Notes
text:
新增一篇笔记
在已有主题的文件夹中，新建一个 .qmd 文件并填写 title、description 和 order。例如：
---
title: "Examples"
description: "Examples illustrating the main definitions and geometric intuition."
order: 45
---
文件保存后，不需要修改 _quarto.yml 或主题的 index.qmd：新页面会自动出现在侧边栏、主题目录和生成的网站中。

title: How to Edit These Notes
text:
新增一个大主题
新建一个主题文件夹，并在其中创建 index.qmd。文件夹名称最好使用小写英文和连字符，例如 perfectoid-spaces。主题首页可以使用下面的模板：
---
title: "Perfectoid Spaces"
subtitle: ""
description: "Notes on perfectoid spaces and their applications."
order: 30
start-page: "perfectoid-spaces/first-note.qmd"
toc: false
listing:
  id: topic-pages
  contents: "*.qmd"
  template: "../_templates/topic-pages.ejs.md"
  fields: [title, description, order]
  sort: "order asc"
  sort-ui: false
  filter-ui: false
---

Write the introduction to this topic here.

## Contents

::: {#topic-pages}
:::
其中 start-page 是首页卡片上 “Start reading” 指向的第一篇笔记。创建主题首页和第一篇笔记后，新主题会自动出现在网站首页与侧边栏中。






Tip最省事的工作方式



你也可以复制同一主题中的现有 .qmd，只修改文件名、页面信息和正文。只要 title、description 和 order 完整，目录不需要手工维护。

title: How to Edit These Notes
text:
本地预览
在英文路径的工作目录 C:\notes\p-adic-geometry-note 中打开 VS Code，然后在终端运行：
.\preview-local.ps1
终端会显示一个 http://localhost:... 地址。保持这个终端运行，保存 .qmd 文件后网页会自动刷新；结束预览时按 Ctrl+C。
确认预览无误后，把修改 commit 并 push 到 main。GitHub Actions 会重新构建并发布网站。

NoteCourse Information




Course Code: MATH70008.01
Course Title: Selected Topics in Representation Theory (Linear Algebraic Groups)
Institution: Shanghai Center for Mathematical Sciences (SCMS), Fudan University
Instructor: Prof. Miaofen Chen (陈苗芬)
Credits: 3.0 (54 Total Credit Hours)

title: Overview
text:
Course Overview
Linear algebraic groups are fundamental objects and tools in mathematics, with wide applications in number theory, representation theory, automorphic forms, and dynamical systems on homogeneous spaces.
The goal of this course is to systematically develop the theory of linear algebraic groups, focusing on their structural properties, representations, and root-theoretic classifications, laying a solid foundation for research in arithmetic geometry, the Langlands program, and related areas.

title: Overview
text:
Syllabus & Lecture Schedule
The notes are organized according to the 7 main modules of the course:

[Weeks 1–2] Linear Algebraic Groups: Foundations & Jordan Decomposition

Affine varieties and the definition of linear algebraic groups
Subgroups, homomorphisms, and canonical examples (\(\mathrm{GL}_n\), \(\mathrm{SL}_n\), \(\mathrm{Sp}_{2n}\), \(\mathrm{SO}_n\))
Jordan-Chevalley decomposition (additive and multiplicative) in \(\mathrm{GL}(V)\) and in abstract linear algebraic groups



[Weeks 3–4] Tannakian Formalism and Lie Algebras

Group actions on affine coordinate algebras \(\mathcal{O}(G)\) and locally finite representations
Tannakian perspective: reconstructing an algebraic group from its representation category
The Lie algebra \(\mathfrak{g} = \operatorname{Lie}(G)\) as invariant derivations
The adjoint representation \(\mathrm{Ad}: G \to \mathrm{GL}(\mathfrak{g})\)



[Week 5] Tori in Algebraic Groups

Diagonalizable groups and Cartier duality
Character lattice \(X^*(T)\) and cocharacter lattice \(X_*(T)\)
Algebraic tori (split vs. non-split)
Rigidity of tori, centralizers, and normalizers



[Week 6] Quotients of Algebraic Groups

Actions on algebraic varieties, orbits, and stabilizers
Chevalley’s Theorem on constructing subgroups as stabilizers of lines
Existence and geometric construction of homogeneous spaces and quotient varieties \(G/H\)



[Weeks 7–8] Reductive Groups

The radical \(R(G)\) and the unipotent radical \(R_u(G)\)
Definitions and characterizations of semisimple and reductive groups
Action of maximal tori on \(\operatorname{Lie}(G)\) and the root space decomposition
Basic properties of roots and root systems



[Weeks 10–11] Parabolic Subgroups of Reductive Groups

The Borel Fixed-Point Theorem for complete varieties
Maximal connected solvable subgroups (Borel subgroups \(B\))
The flag variety \(G/B\) and its projectivity/completeness
Parabolic subgroups: standard parabolic subgroups and their classification



[Weeks 12–13] Various Decompositions of Reductive Groups

The Bruhat decomposition: \(G = \bigsqcup_{w \in W} B w B\)
Relative root systems and decompositions over non-algebraically closed fields
Connections to the Iwasawa and Cartan decompositions in Lie groups and arithmetic groups

text:

Throughout this section:

Let \(k\) be a fixed base field.
A \(k\)-variety is defined as a reduced, separated scheme of finite type over \(k\).
We denote by \(\mathrm{Sch}/k\) the category of schemes of finite type over \(k\), and by \(\mathrm{Var}/k\) the full subcategory of \(k\)-varieties.

title: Basics of Algebraic Groups
text:
Throughout this section:

Let \(k\) be a fixed base field.
A \(k\)-variety is defined as a reduced, separated scheme of finite type over \(k\).
We denote by \(\mathrm{Sch}/k\) the category of schemes of finite type over \(k\), and by \(\mathrm{Var}/k\) the full subcategory of \(k\)-varieties.
For an affine scheme \(X = \operatorname{Spec} A\), \(A\) is a finitely generated \(k\)-algebra.

title: Basics of Algebraic Groups
section: 1. Group Objects and the Rigidity Lemma
text:
1. Group Objects and the Rigidity Lemma






NoteDefinition x.0.0 (Algebraic Group and Abelian Variety)




An algebraic group over \(k\) is a group object in the category \(\mathrm{Sch}/k\). That is, it is a scheme \(G\) of finite type over \(k\) equipped with \(k\)-morphisms:

Multiplication: \(m: G \times_k G \to G\),
Inverse: \(i: G \to G\),
Identity section: \(e: \operatorname{Spec} k \to G\), satisfying the usual group axioms.

An abelian variety is an algebraic variety \(A \in \mathrm{Var}/k\) which is a proper, geometrically connected group object in \(\mathrm{Sch}/k\).









TipLemma x.0.1 (Smoothness of Geometrically Reduced Groups)



Any geometrically reduced algebraic group \(G\) over \(k\) is smooth. Consequently, its connected components coincide with its irreducible components.


Proof sketch. Since \(G_{\bar{k}}\) is reduced and of finite type over an algebraically closed field, its smooth locus \(\operatorname{Sm}(G_{\bar{k}})\) is open and non-empty. For any closed point \(g \in G(\bar{k})\), the group translation \(L_g: G_{\bar{k}} \to G_{\bar{k}}\) is an automorphism mapping smooth points to smooth points. Transitivity of translations implies that every point of \(G_{\bar{k}}\) is smooth. Thus \(G\) is smooth over \(k\). Because smooth schemes are locally irreducible, the connected components must coincide with the irreducible components. \(\square\)






TipLemma x.0.2 (Rigidity Lemma)



Let \(X, Y, Z\) be varieties over \(k\) with \(X\) proper and geometrically irreducible, and \(Y\) geometrically irreducible. Let \[
f: X \times_k Y \to Z
\] be a \(k\)-morphism. Suppose there exists a \(k\)-rational point \(y_0 \in Y(k)\) such that \(f(X \times \{y_0\}) = \{z_0\}\) for some \(z_0 \in Z(k)\).
Then \(f\) factors through the canonical projection \(p_2: X \times_k Y \to Y\). That is, there exists a morphism \(g: Y \to Z\) such that \(f = g \circ p_2\).


Proof. Fix a rational point \(x_0 \in X(k)\) (extending scalars to \(\bar{k}\) if necessary). Define \(g: Y \to Z\) by the composition: \[
Y \xrightarrow{x_0 \times \mathrm{id}_Y} X \times_k Y \xrightarrow{f} Z.
\] We show that \(f(x, y) = g(y)\) for all \(x \in X, y \in Y\).

Choose an affine open neighborhood \(U \subseteq Z\) containing \(z_0\). The complement \(Z \setminus U\) is closed in \(Z\), so \(f^{-1}(Z \setminus U)\) is closed in \(X \times_k Y\).
Since \(X\) is proper over \(k\), the projection \(p_2: X \times_k Y \to Y\) is universally closed. Thus: \[
W := p_2\big(f^{-1}(Z \setminus U)\big) = \{ y \in Y \mid \exists x \in X \text{ with } f(x, y) \notin U \}
\] is a closed subset of \(Y\).
By hypothesis, \(f(X \times \{y_0\}) = \{z_0\} \subseteq U\), so \(y_0 \notin W\). Hence \(Y \setminus W\) is an open neighborhood of \(y_0\). Pick an affine open neighborhood \(V \subseteq Y \setminus W\) containing \(y_0\).
By construction, \(f(X \times V) \subseteq U\). Since \(U\) is affine, we may choose a closed embedding \(U \hookrightarrow \mathbb{A}^n\). For every closed point \(y \in V\), the fiber \(X \times \{y\} \cong X\) is proper and connected. Its image in the affine space \(\mathbb{A}^n\) under \(f\) must be both proper and affine, hence it must be a single point: \[
f(X \times \{y\}) = \{f(x_0, y)\} = \{g(y)\}.
\]
Therefore, \(f|_{X \times V} = (g \circ p_2)|_{X \times V}\). Because \(X \times_k Y\) is reduced and \(Z\) is separated, two morphisms agreeing on a non-empty open subscheme are identical everywhere (Reduced-to-Separated Theorem). Thus \(f = g \circ p_2\). \(\square\)







ImportantProposition x.0.3 (Proper Connected Groups are Abelian)



Any proper connected smooth algebraic group \(G\) over \(k\) is abelian. In particular, abelian varieties are commutative.


Proof. Consider the commutator morphism: \[
f: G \times_k G \to G, \quad (x, y) \mapsto x y x^{-1} y^{-1}.
\] Observe that \(f(G \times \{e\}) = \{e\}\). Since \(G\) is proper and connected, Lemma x.0.2 (Rigidity) implies that \(f\) factors through the projection to the second factor: \[
f(x, y) = f(e, y) = e y e^{-1} y^{-1} = e.
\] Hence \(xyx^{-1}y^{-1} = e\) for all \(x, y \in G\), meaning \(xy = yx\). Thus \(G\) is abelian. \(\square\)

title: Basics of Algebraic Groups
text:
2. Topological and Subgroup Properties






ImportantProposition x.0.4 (Separatedness of Group Schemes)



Every group scheme \(G\) of finite type over a field \(k\) is separated.


Proof. A morphism \(G \to \operatorname{Spec} k\) is separated if and only if the diagonal \(\Delta: G \to G \times_k G\) is a closed immersion.
Consider the difference morphism \(\mu: G \times_k G \to G\) defined by \((g_1, g_2) \mapsto g_1 g_2^{-1}\). The diagonal \(\Delta(G)\) is the scheme-theoretic pullback of the identity section \(e: \operatorname{Spec} k \to G\) along \(\mu\): \[
\begin{matrix}
G & \xrightarrow{\Delta} & G \times_k G \\
\downarrow & \square & \downarrow \mu \\
\operatorname{Spec} k & \xrightarrow{e} & G
\end{matrix}
\] Because base change preserves closed immersions, it suffices to prove that \(e: \operatorname{Spec} k \to G\) is a closed immersion. The image of \(e\) is a single point \(e \in G\). Since \(G\) is of finite type over \(k\), the point \(e\) has residue field \(k(e) \cong k\) and is closed. Thus \(e\) is a closed immersion, which implies \(\Delta\) is a closed immersion. Therefore, \(G\) is separated over \(k\). \(\square\)






TipLemma x.0.5 (Open Subgroups are Closed)




If \(G\) is a group scheme over \(k\) such that \(G_{\mathrm{red}} \times_k G_{\mathrm{red}}\) is reduced, then \(G_{\mathrm{red}} \hookrightarrow G\) is a closed subgroup scheme.
Let \(\varphi: G' \to G\) be a homomorphism of group schemes over \(k\). If the image \(\varphi(G')\) is open in \(G\), then \(\varphi(G')\) is also closed in \(G\).



Proof of (2). Let \(U = \varphi(G') \subseteq G\) be open. Endow the complement \(Z := G \setminus U\) with the reduced subscheme structure. It suffices to show that \(Z\) is open.
Consider the action map \(Z \times_k G' \to G\) given by \((z, g') \mapsto z \cdot \varphi(g')\). For any \(g' \in G'\), the translation \(x \mapsto x \cdot \varphi(g')\) is an automorphism of \(G\). Since \(U = \varphi(G')\) is stable under right multiplication by \(\varphi(G')\), its complement \(Z\) is also stable under multiplication by \(\varphi(G')\).
Because translations are open morphisms, the image of \(Z \times_k G' \to G\) is a union of translates of \(Z\), which is open. But this image is precisely \(Z\) itself. Hence \(Z\) is open, which proves \(U = G \setminus Z\) is closed. \(\square\)






TipLemma x.0.6 (Immersions of Group Schemes are Closed)



Let \(i: G' \hookrightarrow G\) be an immersion of group schemes over \(k\). Then \(i\) is a closed immersion.


Proof. Without loss of generality, assume \(G\) and \(G'\) are reduced. Let \(\overline{G'}\) denote the scheme-theoretic closure of \(i(G')\) in \(G\) equipped with the reduced structure. Since multiplication \(m: G \times_k G \to G\) is continuous and maps \(G' \times_k G'\) into \(G'\), it maps the closure \(\overline{G'} \times_k \overline{G'}\) into \(\overline{G'}\). Thus \(\overline{G'}\) is a closed subgroup scheme of \(G\).
Since \(i\) is an immersion, \(i(G')\) is an open subscheme of \(\overline{G'}\). By Lemma x.0.5, an open subgroup scheme of \(\overline{G'}\) is closed in \(\overline{G'}\). Hence \(i(G') = \overline{G'}\), so \(i(G')\) is closed in \(G\). \(\square\)






TipLemma x.0.7 (Connected Implies Irreducible)



Let \(G\) be a group scheme of finite type over \(k\). 1. If \(G\) is irreducible, then \(G\) is quasi-compact. 2. If \(G\) is connected, then \(G\) is irreducible.


(Reference: The Stacks Project, Tag 047R, Tag 047S).

title: Basics of Algebraic Groups
text:
3. Kernels, Images, and Homomorphisms






NoteDefinition & Proposition x.0.8 (Subgroup Schemes and Kernels)




A closed subscheme \(H \subseteq G\) is a normal subgroup scheme (denoted \(H \trianglelefteq G\)) if for all \(T \in \mathrm{Sch}/k\), \(H(T)\) is a normal subgroup of \(G(T)\) (equivalently, \(H(R) \trianglelefteq G(R)\) for all \(R \in \mathrm{Alg}_k\)).
Let \(\varphi: G \to G'\) be a homomorphism of group schemes. The scheme-theoretic kernel is defined as the fiber product: \[
\ker \varphi := \operatorname{Spec} k \times_{e, G', \varphi} G = \varphi^{-1}(e).
\] Then \(\ker \varphi\) is a closed normal subgroup scheme of \(G\).
On functor of points, \(\ker(\varphi)(R) = \ker(G(R) \to G'(R))\) for all \(R \in \mathrm{Alg}_k\).









ImportantProposition x.0.9 (Homomorphisms and Dimensions)



Let \(\varphi: G \to G'\) be a homomorphism of algebraic groups over \(k\). 1. The scheme-theoretic image \(\varphi(G)\) is closed in \(G'\). We denote \(\operatorname{Im} \varphi := \varphi(G)_{\mathrm{red}}\). 2. Dimension Formula: \[
   \dim G = \dim \ker \varphi + \dim \operatorname{Im} \varphi.
   \] 3. \(\varphi: G \to \operatorname{Im} \varphi\) is smooth if and only if \(\ker \varphi\) is geometrically reduced, if and only if the differential \(d\varphi_e: T_e(G) \to T_e(\operatorname{Im} \varphi)\) is surjective.


Idea of Proof. By Chevalley’s Theorem on constructible sets, \(\varphi(G)\) contains a dense open subset of its closure. Group translations then show that \(\varphi(G)\) is open in its closure \(\overline{\varphi(G)}\). By Lemma x.0.5, an open subgroup of \(\overline{\varphi(G)}\) is closed, whence \(\varphi(G) = \overline{\varphi(G)}\). \(\square\)






ImportantProposition x.0.10 (Image Factorization and Flatness)




If \(G'\) is reduced and \(\varphi: G \to G'\) is dominant, then \(\varphi\) is an fppf morphism (faithfully flat of finite presentation).
If \(G\) is smooth, any homomorphism \(\varphi: G \to H\) factors canonically as: \[
G \xrightarrow{p} I \xrightarrow{i} H
\] where \(p\) is fppf and \(i\) is a closed immersion into \(H\).



Proof. Set \(I := \varphi(G)\) with reduced subscheme structure. By generic flatness, there exists a dense open subscheme \(U \subseteq I\) over which \(\varphi^{-1}(U) \to U\) is flat. Since translations by rational points (over \(\bar{k}\)) act transitively on \(I\), translates of \(U\) cover \(I\). Therefore, \(\varphi\) is flat everywhere. Being surjective and of finite type, it is fppf. \(\square\)






NoteDefinition x.0.11 (The Identity Component \(G^\circ\))




The identity component \(G^\circ\) of an algebraic group \(G\) is the connected component containing the identity section \(e\). Endowed with its open subscheme structure, \(G^\circ\) is a smooth, geometrically connected, open and closed normal subgroup scheme of \(G\).
For any open subgroup \(G' \subseteq G\) of finite index, \(G^\circ \subseteq G' \subseteq G\), and \((G^\circ)^\circ = G^\circ\).

title: Basics of Algebraic Groups
section: 4. Affine Algebraic Groups and Hopf Algebras
text:
4. Affine Algebraic Groups and Hopf Algebras






NoteRemark x.0.12 (Hopf Algebras and Functor of Points)



An affine scheme \(G = \operatorname{Spec} A\) is a group scheme if and only if its coordinate ring \(A = \mathcal{O}(G)\) is a commutative Hopf algebra over \(k\), equipped with: - Comultiplication \(\Delta: A \to A \otimes_k A\), - Counit \(\varepsilon: A \to k\), - Antipode \(S: A \to A\).
We have an anti-equivalence of categories: \[
\{\text{Commutative f.g. Hopf } k\text{-algebras}\}^{\mathrm{op}} \xrightarrow{\sim} \{\text{Affine / Linear } k\text{-algebraic groups}\}.
\] Via the functor of points, the Yoneda embedding yields a fully faithful functor: \[
\mathbf{GrpSch}/k \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Fun}(\mathrm{Alg}_k, \mathbf{Grp}), \quad G \mapsto (R \mapsto G(R) = \operatorname{Hom}_{k\text{-alg}}(A, R)).
\]








NoteExample x.0.13 (Basic Examples)




Finite Constant Group: Let \(\Gamma\) be a finite abstract group. The coordinate algebra is \(A = \prod_{g \in \Gamma} k \cdot e_g\) with orthogonal idempotents \(e_g\).

Comultiplication: \(\Delta(e_x) = \sum_{yz = x} e_y \otimes e_z\),
Antipode: \(S(e_x) = e_{x^{-1}}\),
Counit: \(\varepsilon(e_x) = \delta_{x, e}\). On \(R\)-points: \(G(R) = \{ (r_g)_{g \in \Gamma} \in R^\Gamma \mid \sum r_g = 1, \, r_g r_h = 0 \text{ for } g \neq h \}\).

Standard Matrix Groups (for \(n \in \mathbb{N}\)):

General Linear Group \(\mathrm{GL}_n\) (Reductive): \[
\mathrm{GL}_n(R) = \{ M \in \mathrm{Mat}_{n \times n}(R) \mid \det(M) \in R^\times \}.
\]
Standard Borel Subgroup \(B_n\) (Solvable): \[
B_n(R) = \{ (x_{ij}) \in \mathrm{GL}_n(R) \mid x_{ij} = 0 \text{ for all } i > j \}.
\]
Standard Unipotent Subgroup \(U_n\) (Unipotent): \[
U_n(R) = \{ (x_{ij}) \in B_n(R) \mid x_{ii} = 1 \text{ for all } 1 \le i \le n \}.
\]
Standard Maximal Torus \(T_n\) (Split Torus): \[
T_n(R) = \{ (x_{ij}) \in B_n(R) \mid x_{ij} = 0 \text{ for all } i \neq j \} \cong (\mathbb{G}_{m, R})^n.
\] These satisfy the inclusion hierarchy: \[
U_n \trianglelefteq B_n \subseteq \mathrm{GL}_n, \quad T_n \subseteq B_n, \quad B_n = T_n \ltimes U_n.
\]










TipProposition x.0.14 (Reduction of Group Schemes)



Let \(G\) be an algebraic group over \(k\). If \(G_{\mathrm{red}}\) is geometrically reduced (e.g., if \(k\) is perfect), then \(G_{\mathrm{red}} \hookrightarrow G\) is a smooth closed subgroup scheme of \(G\).

title: Basics of Algebraic Groups
section: 5. The Étale Quotient \(\pi_0(X)\) and Component Groups
text:
5. The Étale Quotient \(\pi_0(X)\) and Component Groups






ImportantProposition x.0.15 (Existence of the Largest Étale Subalgebra)



Let \(X\) be a scheme of finite type over \(k\). Then there exists a unique largest étale \(k\)-subalgebra \(\pi_0(X) \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X)\).


Proof. 1. If \(A_1, A_2 \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X)\) are étale \(k\)-subalgebras, the subring generated by them is the image of the canonical map \(A_1 \otimes_k A_2 \to \mathcal{O}(X)\). Since the tensor product of étale algebras is étale and any quotient of an étale algebra over a field is étale, the composite is étale. 2. For any étale subalgebra \(A \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X)\), base change to the separable closure satisfies: \[
   A \otimes_k k^{\mathrm{sep}} \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X) \otimes_k k^{\mathrm{sep}} = \mathcal{O}(X_{k^{\mathrm{sep}}}).
   \] Since \(A \otimes_k k^{\mathrm{sep}} \cong \prod_{i=1}^m k^{\mathrm{sep}}\), it admits a complete system of orthogonal idempotents \(e_1, \dots, e_m\). Each \(e_i\) defines a non-empty open and closed subscheme \(V(1 - e_i)\) of \(X_{k^{\mathrm{sep}}}\). Thus \(m \le \#\{\text{connected components of } X_{k^{\mathrm{sep}}}\}\). 3. Because \(X\) is of finite type, it has finitely many connected components. The dimension \(\dim_k A\) is uniformly bounded, guaranteeing the existence of a unique maximal étale subalgebra. \(\square\)






NoteDefinition x.0.16 (The Scheme \(\pi_0(X)\))




Let \(A \subseteq \mathcal{O}(X)\) be the largest étale \(k\)-subalgebra. We define: \[
\pi_0(X) := \operatorname{Spec} A.
\] The inclusion \(A \hookrightarrow \mathcal{O}(X)\) induces a canonical morphism \(X \to \pi_0(X)\).
Universal Property: For any étale \(k\)-scheme \(Y\) and any \(k\)-morphism \(f: X \to Y\), there exists a unique morphism \(\bar{f}: \pi_0(X) \to Y\) making the diagram commute: \[
\begin{matrix}
X & \xrightarrow{f} & Y \\
\downarrow & \nearrow_{\exists! \bar{f}} & \\
\pi_0(X) & &
\end{matrix}
\]
Properties:

The fibers of \(X \to \pi_0(X)\) are the connected components of \(X\).
For every \(y \in \pi_0(X)\), the fiber \(X_y\) is geometrically connected over the residue field \(k(y)\).
\(\pi_0\) preserves finite products: \(\pi_0(X \times_k Y) \cong \pi_0(X) \times_k \pi_0(Y)\).
The canonical morphism \(X \to \pi_0(X)\) is fppf.










TipProposition x.0.17 (Geometric Connectedness Criteria)




If \(X\) is connected and \(X(k) \neq \emptyset\), then \(X\) is geometrically connected.
If \(X\) is geometrically connected and \(Y\) is connected, then \(X \times_k Y\) is connected.



Proof. 1. If \(X\) is connected, \(\pi_0(X) = \operatorname{Spec} L\), where \(L/k\) is a finite separable field extension. A rational point \(x \in X(k)\) provides a section \(\operatorname{Spec} k \to X \to \operatorname{Spec} L\), forcing \(L \cong k\). Thus \(\pi_0(X) = \operatorname{Spec} k\), so \(X\) is geometrically connected. 2. We have \(\pi_0(X) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k\). By product preservation, \(\pi_0(X \times_k Y) \cong \pi_0(X) \times_k \pi_0(Y) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k \times_k \pi_0(Y) \cong \pi_0(Y)\). Since \(Y\) is connected, \(\pi_0(Y) = \operatorname{Spec} L\) for a field \(L\). Thus \(\pi_0(X \times_k Y) \cong \operatorname{Spec} L\), which shows \(X \times_k Y\) is connected. \(\square\)






ImportantProposition x.0.18 (\(\pi_0(G)\) and the Connected Component)



Let \(G\) be an algebraic group over \(k\). 1. \(\pi_0(G)\) is a finite étale group scheme over \(k\), and the canonical morphism \(G \to \pi_0(G)\) is a homomorphism of algebraic groups. 2. The identity component \(G^\circ := \ker(G \to \pi_0(G))\) is a geometrically connected, normal closed and open subgroup scheme of \(G\). For any field extension \(L/k\), we have \((G_L)^\circ = (G^\circ)_L\). 3. \(G\) is connected \(\iff \pi_0(G) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k \iff G\) is geometrically connected. 4. Formation of the identity component commutes with products: \((G \times_k H)^\circ \cong G^\circ \times_k H^\circ\). 5. If \(H\) is a connected group scheme over \(k\), any homomorphism \(\psi: H \to G\) factors uniquely through \(G^\circ \hookrightarrow G\).


Proof. - Since \(\pi_0\) commutes with finite products, the group morphisms \(m, i, e\) on \(G\) induce group structure morphisms on \(\pi_0(G)\) by functoriality. - For (3), since \(e \in G^\circ(k)\), \(G^\circ\) has a \(k\)-rational point. Proposition x.0.17(1) implies that \(G^\circ\) is geometrically connected. - For (5), since \(H\) is connected, \(\pi_0(H) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k\). Functoriality yields a commutative diagram: \[
  \begin{matrix}
  H & \xrightarrow{\psi} & G \\
  \downarrow & & \downarrow \\
  \pi_0(H) \cong \operatorname{Spec} k & \xrightarrow{e} & \pi_0(G)
  \end{matrix}
  \] Thus the composition \(H \to G \to \pi_0(G)\) is the trivial map, which implies that \(\psi\) factors uniquely through \(G^\circ = \ker(G \to \pi_0(G))\). \(\square\)






NoteDefinition x.0.19 (Exact Sequences of Group Schemes)



A sequence of homomorphisms of group schemes over \(k\): \[
1 \longrightarrow N \xrightarrow{\quad i \quad} G \xrightarrow{\quad p \quad} Q \longrightarrow 1
\] is said to be exact if: 1. \(i: N \hookrightarrow G\) is a closed immersion identifying \(N\) with a normal subgroup scheme of \(G\); 2. \(p: G \to Q\) is an fppf quotient morphism; 3. \(i(N) = \ker(p)\) scheme-theoretically.
